715.title: The great persecution (303)
715.hook: Diocletian orders churches destroyed and scriptures burned
715.howItsDone: Catholics honor the martyrs of this persecution in the Church's calendar, and the Church still asks the faithful to pray for Christians who suffer for their faith today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Agnes, too small for the chains, whose name sounds like lamb. Your line was the lamb.

At first light, soldiers and officials force open the doors of a church. It stands in Nicomedia, the city where the emperor Diocletian keeps his court, and the emperors watch from the palace. Inside, the officials search for an image of God and find none. They find the scriptures, and burn them. They take what they want. Then the guard comes in with axes and tools, and in a few hours the building is flat. The writer Lactantius tells it this way. It's the opening scene of what Christians came to call the great persecution.
screen: `AT FIRST LIGHT.` → `THE EMPERORS WATCH.` → `THE SCRIPTURES BURN.`

segments.voice: First, the order. Lactantius says an edict came out the next day. Christians lost their rank and their protection under the law. Eusebius, the historian, says the imperial letters ordered churches torn down to their foundations and the scriptures destroyed by fire. Second, the fire in the square. Eusebius writes that he saw it with his own eyes: houses of prayer thrown down, and the holy scriptures burned in the middle of the marketplaces. Not a rumor. A thing he watched. Third, the people who said no. In a town in North Africa, the officials came to Bishop Felix and demanded the church's books. The account of his trial gives his answer, simply: I have them, but I won't give them up. He was put to death for it. Others hid the books, or handed over something else in their place. Fourth, the people who said yes. Some clergy did hand the books over to save their lives. Christians in North Africa called them traditores, those who handed over, and the arguments about whether they could still serve as priests and bishops ran on long after the danger was gone. It's an uncomfortable part of the story, and an honest one: courage and fear in the same churches. Tradition places Agnes, from yesterday, in this same storm.

segments.voice: If there's a Bible or a prayer book near you, put your hand on it, or picture one on a shelf, and notice how ordinary it is to own it. Then think of people for whom it isn't ordinary: keeping a few pages hidden, reading at night, sharing a single copy with friends, afraid of a knock at the door. If you pray, ask for a safe place for them to read.
traditores. Latin for those who handed over, the name given to Christians who gave up the scriptures under the great persecution. Today's word.
Your line: they hid the books. Some paid with their lives to keep them. Day seven hundred fifteen.

716.title: Constantine (312–313)
716.hook: the emperor's victory, the Edict of Milan, and a freedom that brought new temptations
716.howItsDone: In Catholic tellings of Church history, Constantine's reign marks the end of the great persecution and the start of the Church's public life in the empire, with new freedom and new temptations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the great persecution, and the traditores who handed the books over. Your line was they hid the books.

Two Christian writers of the emperor's own time tell the same story, and they don't tell it the same way. Constantine is marching on Rome to fight a rival for the throne. Lactantius says he was told in a dream to mark the heavenly sign of God on his soldiers' shields, and he did. Eusebius, writing later, says Constantine told him, and swore to it, that he saw a sign of light in the sky, a cross above the sun, with words: by this, conquer. Either way, he wins. And the world of the persecuted Church turns upside down.
screen: `TWO WRITERS, ONE STORY.` → `A SIGN ON THE SHIELDS.` → `BY THIS, CONQUER.`

segments.voice: First, the sign. It's honest to say the sources differ: a dream in one, a vision in the sky and then a dream in the other. What they agree on is that Constantine put a Christian sign on his army, and credited his victory to Christ. Second, the letter. Afterward, Constantine and his fellow emperor Licinius agree on a policy, and Lactantius copies the letter that announces it. It grants to Christians, and to all others, the free choice to follow whatever worship each person wants. Church buildings and property taken in the persecution are to be given back. People call it the Edict of Milan. Remember Nicomedia, and the books burning in the market square. Now Christians can ask for their churches back. Third, the surprise. Freedom was a gift, and it came with new temptations. The emperor gave the church money, buildings and favor. Bishops found themselves near the throne. Being Christian became useful for a career. Eusebius himself, who admired Constantine, complains in his Life of Constantine about hypocrites who slipped into the Church to win the emperor's goodwill. And Constantine, Eusebius says, was baptized only near the end of his life. Fourth, why it matters now. Persecution asks one question: will you stay? Comfort asks a quieter one: why are you here? The Church after Constantine had to learn to answer the second question.
screen: `TWO TELLINGS OF ONE SIGN.` · `FREEDOM FOR CHRISTIANS AND ALL OTHERS.` · `NEW TEMPTATIONS.` · `WHY ARE YOU HERE?` · then, large: `FREEDOM, AND ITS DANGERS.`

segments.voice: Think back to a stretch of your life when things were hard, then one when things were easy, and notice where your attention was in each: on God, on the people you love, on what matters most. Don't judge it; just notice what changed. Then look at today: is anything comfortable crowding out something that matters? If you pray, bring that to God honestly.
Constantine. The emperor who won under a Christian sign, granted freedom of worship, and brought the Church both peace and new temptations. Today's word.
Your line: freedom, and its dangers. Tomorrow, the emperor's mother takes the road east. Day seven hundred sixteen, done.

717.title: Helena in Jerusalem
717.hook: the emperor's mother builds churches at the holy places; tradition says she found the cross
717.howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Helena as a saint, and pilgrims still travel to the churches at the holy places in Bethlehem and Jerusalem; parishes often take up collections for Christians in the Holy Land.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Constantine: an emperor's victory, and a Church suddenly free to worship in the open. Your line was freedom, and its dangers.

The emperor's mother is packing for a long road east. Her name is Helena, and her son is Constantine. She could send architects. She could send gold and a letter with the imperial seal. Instead she goes herself, to the land where the Gospels happened. Bishop Eusebius, who wrote a life of her son, says she went to give thanks and to pray in the places where the Savior had walked. Not a tour of inspection. A pilgrimage.
screen: `THE EMPEROR'S MOTHER.` → `SHE COULD HAVE SENT GOLD.` → `SHE WENT HERSELF.`

segments.voice: Start with what Eusebius tells us. Helena dedicated two churches: one over the cave at Bethlehem where, Christians said, Jesus was born, and one on the Mount of Olives, at the place of the ascension. The aim was to mark the spots where God had come close, so pilgrims could stand there too. Second, the road. Eusebius says she gave freely as she traveled: to whole towns, to soldiers, to people with nothing to wear, to prisoners, some of whom she set free. In church she didn't sit apart in imperial splendor. She came in plain clothes and prayed among ordinary worshippers. Third, the story that travels with her name. Tradition says that in Jerusalem Helena searched for the cross of Christ, and found it. Here it helps to be honest about the sources. Eusebius, who describes her journey and her churches, says nothing about a cross. The story of the finding appears in later writers, among them Saint Ambrose of Milan. The Church honors relics of the cross, and the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross recalls them. Catholics and Orthodox Christians honor Helena as a saint, whatever a historian decides about the details. Fourth, why her trip still matters. In Luke's Gospel, after the angels leave, the shepherds say: "Let us go over to Bethlehem, and let us see this word that is come to pass." Eusebius says Helena made her journey in old age. Like the shepherds, she didn't settle for hearing about it. She went to see. And Christians still live in Bethlehem, Jerusalem and Nazareth, and still pray in churches near the places she marked.
screen: `TWO CHURCHES SHE BUILT.` · `GIFTS ALONG THE ROAD.` · `TRADITION SAYS: THE CROSS.` · `LET US GO OVER TO BETHLEHEM.` · then, large: `SHE WENT TO SEE.`

segments.voice: Picture Bethlehem, Jerusalem and Nazareth, towns where Christian families worship near the old holy places, alongside neighbors of other faiths: one street, one church door, one family getting ready for Sunday. If you pray, pray for Christians in the Holy Land and for peace for everyone who lives there; if you don't, simply keep them in mind, one town at a time.

718.title: Anthony of the desert (c. 251–356)
718.hook: hearing the gospel of the rich young man, he sells everything and goes into the desert
718.howItsDone: Catholic monks and nuns live under vows in monasteries, praying together through the day, and the Church keeps the feast of Saint Anthony the Abbot each year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Helena built churches at Bethlehem and on the Mount of Olives. Your line was she went to see.

A young man in Egypt is walking to church. His parents have died. He's been left land, and a younger sister to look after. He's thinking about the apostles, who left everything to follow Jesus, and the believers in Acts, who sold what they had and laid the money at the apostles' feet. He walks in just as the Gospel is being read. It's the story of the rich young man. His name is Anthony, and what he does next starts something.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN WITH LAND.` → `THINKING ABOUT THE APOSTLES.` → `THE GOSPEL IS BEING READ.`

segments.voice: Here's the line he heard, in the Douay-Rheims: "If thou wilt be perfect, go sell what thou hast, and give to the poor." In the Gospel, the rich young man goes away sad. Anthony's biographer, Saint Athanasius, says Anthony heard it as if it had been read for him alone. So he did what the young man couldn't. He gave his family's land to the people of his village, sold the rest and gave the money to the poor, keeping a little back for his sister. Then, the story goes, he walked into church another day and heard Jesus say not to be anxious about tomorrow. So he gave away the rest, and placed his sister with a community of women who had given their lives to God. Next, the desert. He didn't vanish all at once. Athanasius says he first learned from an old man near his village, copying the good habits of people around him: one in prayer, another in kindness, another in fasting. Then he went farther out, to tombs, to an empty fort, and at last into the mountains, praying, working with his hands, and struggling, in Athanasius's telling, against temptations that came at him like enemies. Then the strange part. He went to be alone, and people followed him, for advice, for healing, for a word. Some stayed and built huts nearby. Athanasius says the desert became like a city, filled with monks. A monk is someone who leaves ordinary life to live for God in prayer, alone or with others. Catholic monks and nuns still do, in monasteries around the world. Tradition calls Anthony the father of monks.
screen: `IF THOU WILT BE PERFECT.` · `HE GAVE IT AWAY.` · `FARTHER INTO THE DESERT.` · `THE DESERT FILLS WITH MONKS.` · then, large: `HE HEARD AND WENT.`

segments.voice: Nobody is asking you to sell the house. Let your mind find one thing at home you don't need that someone else could use, a coat, a book, and notice whether there's a small tug of wanting to keep it. If there is, that tug is where Anthony's story lives; if you pray, offer the thing, and the tug, to God.
Monk. Someone who leaves ordinary life to live for God in prayer, alone or with others. Today's word.

719.title: Sit in your cell
719.hook: a desert father's advice: sit in your cell and your cell will teach you everything
719.howItsDone: Catholic monks and nuns keep times of silence in their cells and cloisters, and many lay Catholics set aside a quiet place at home for prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anthony heard one Gospel line in church and walked into the desert. Your word was monk, and your line was he heard and went.

A brother has crossed the desert to Scetis to see an old monk called Abba Moses. He asks what visitors to the desert asked: give me a word, one saying to live by. Perhaps he expects something hard. Fasting. Vigils. A rule. The old man answers with one sentence. Go, sit in your cell, and your cell will teach you everything. That's all. No program. No follow-up. A word that sounds too simple to work.
screen: `GIVE ME A WORD.` → `ONE SAYING TO LIVE BY.` → `GO, SIT IN YOUR CELL.`

segments.voice: Start with the title. The visitor calls him abba. It's the word for father, and Christians knew it from the Gospel: in Gethsemane, in Mark's telling, Jesus prays, "Abba, Father." In the desert, abba became the name for an elder whose life gave his words weight. Those short sayings were gathered into the collection we call the Sayings of the Desert Fathers. Next, the man. Tradition says Abba Moses had a rough past before he became a monk, and the sayings remember him for humility. Once, they say, the brothers called a meeting to judge a monk who had sinned. Moses at first refused to come. When they sent for him again, he came carrying a leaking jug of water. Asked why, he said his own sins were running out behind him where he couldn't see them, and here he was, coming to judge someone else's. The brothers said no more, and forgave the one who had sinned. Third, the cell. A monk's cell wasn't a prison. It was his small hut or room, where he prayed, slept and worked. So why would a room teach everything? Some readers hear it this way: when you stop going elsewhere, you meet what you brought with you. Restlessness. Boredom. The itch to check on something, anything. The urge to leave. On that reading, those aren't distractions from the lesson. They are the lesson. Staying put, the sayings suggest, lets you see yourself without the usual escape routes, and that's where prayer starts to get honest. Fourth, your own cell: a kitchen, a bedroom, a parked car, a desk at lunch. The advice travels.
screen: `ABBA: FATHER.` · `THE LEAKING JUG.` · `A CELL IS A SMALL ROOM.` · `YOUR OWN CELL.` · then, large: `THE CELL TEACHES.`

segments.voice: Wherever you are, that's your cell: don't get up, don't tidy, don't reach for the phone. Notice what wants to leave first, your hands, your eyes, your thoughts, and just stay. If you pray, say the two words from Gethsemane, Abba, Father, and let the rest be quiet; if not, let your breath be the only thing that moves.
Abba. Father: the word Jesus prays in Gethsemane, and the name the desert gave its elders. Today's word.
Your line: the cell teaches. Even a small room can be enough, if you stay. Until tomorrow.

720.title: The desert mothers
720.hook: Amma Syncletica and others taught that the real desert is the heart
720.howItsDone: Catholic women religious, including contemplative nuns, continue a life of prayer and silence, and the Church honors Saint Syncletica among the desert mothers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abba Moses told a visitor to go and sit in his cell. Your word was abba, and your line was the cell teaches.

Turn the pages of the desert sayings and the title you keep meeting is abba. Abba this, abba that. Then, here and there, a different one. Amma Sarah. Amma Theodora. Amma Syncletica. Women who went out to pray in the wilderness too, remembered not as someone's sister or helper, but as teachers in their own right. People came to them asking for a word, just as they did with the men. And one of them moved the desert somewhere nobody expected.
screen: `ABBA, ABBA, ABBA.` → `THEN: AMMA.` → `TEACHERS IN THEIR OWN RIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, the title. Amma means mother. Like abba, it's not a family tie but a spiritual one: an elder whose life had taught her something worth passing on, and whose few words people carried home. Second, one of them by name. Tradition says Syncletica came from a well-off family in Alexandria, gave away what she had, and lived a life of prayer and fasting near the city, not deep in the sand. Younger women gathered to learn from her, and a later writer collected her teaching into a life. Her sayings sit right beside the abbas' in the desert collection. Third, the turn. A desert mother might be expected to say: go to the desert. Syncletica says something sharper. Some who live out on the mountain, she warns, behave as if they were in town, and they're lost. And it's possible to live among a crowd and be solitary in your mind, while someone living alone can be living in a crowd of her own thoughts. The quiet isn't guaranteed by the sand. The noise isn't guaranteed by the city. For Syncletica, the real desert, the place of prayer without distraction, is inside. Fourth, what that means on a Tuesday: a bus, a waiting room, a kitchen at dinnertime. The desert mothers didn't promise those places would go quiet. Syncletica's saying suggests the quiet can be found in them anyway, and that a person can carry a small wilderness through a loud day.
screen: `AMMA: MOTHER.` · `SYNCLETICA OF ALEXANDRIA.` · `A CROWD IN YOUR OWN THOUGHTS.` · `A DESERT YOU CAN CARRY.` · then, large: `THE DESERT IS WITHIN.`

segments.voice: Leave the noise around you as it is, traffic, voices, a fridge humming, and notice the crowd of your own thoughts, the way Syncletica describes it. Don't chase them out; step back from them, the way you'd step off a busy street onto a doorstep. If you pray, rest in God's presence without saying anything at all.
Amma. Mother: the title the desert gave its women teachers, like Amma Syncletica. Today's word.
Your line: the desert is within. The quiet can travel with you. That's day seven hundred twenty.

721.title: Pachomius
721.hook: a former soldier organizes monks into communities with shared work and prayer
721.howItsDone: Catholic monks and nuns who live in community share meals, work and the prayer of the hours under a rule and a superior, and the Church honors Saint Pachomius as a founder of that common life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the desert mothers, and Amma Syncletica's warning that a crowd can live inside your head. Your word was amma, and your line was the desert is within.

Down the Nile goes a boatload of new recruits, kept under guard at night, more like prisoners than soldiers. One of them is a young Egyptian, just drafted into the army. At one town, strangers come down to the boat with food and drink and look after them. He asks who these people are. Christians, he's told: kind to everyone, for the sake of God. That night, the story of his life says, he made a promise: if he got free, he would serve God and serve people. His name is Pachomius.
screen: `DRAFTED, UNDER GUARD.` → `STRANGERS BRING FOOD.` → `A PROMISE THAT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, the kindness keeps working. Released from the army, Pachomius is baptized and goes to learn the desert life from an old hermit named Palamon. Hard teaching: little food, long prayer, manual work. Second, the new thing. Anthony's way, three days ago, was mostly the hermit's way, alone or nearly. Pachomius gathers monks into a community. At a deserted village called Tabennesi, the story goes, he begins to build. One wall around them all. One rule. One table. The monks weave mats and baskets, farm, cook and nurse the sick, and what they make is for everyone. They pray together at set times. An abbot leads, and the brothers obey him, not as a general but as a father. Third, why it matters. The hermit's life suits a few. A shared life can hold many: the strong and the weak, the gifted and the ordinary. Some readers see in his communities the picture in Acts, where the believers held all things in common. Shared work can wear off rough edges in a way solitude may not, because the brother who annoys you is at breakfast tomorrow. Catholic religious orders that live in community stand in that line. Fourth, look back at this week. Under persecution, they hid the books. With Constantine came freedom, and its dangers. Helena went to see. Anthony heard and went. Abba Moses said the cell teaches. Syncletica said the desert is within. And Pachomius says what the desert needed to hear: you don't have to go alone.
screen: `A HERMIT'S HARD SCHOOL.` · `ONE WALL, ONE RULE, ONE TABLE.` · `THE BROTHER AT BREAKFAST.` · `THIS WEEK, LOOKING BACK.` · then, large: `TOGETHER IN THE DESERT.`

segments.voice: Think through the work of your day, dishes, a report, a ride to school, a meal, and pick one task you usually do alone. Picture doing it beside someone instead, not handing it off but side by side, the way Pachomius's monks wove and cooked together. If you pray, ask a blessing on the work you share.
Pachomius. A former soldier, won over by strangers' kindness, who gathered monks into communities of shared work and prayer. Today's word.
Your line: together in the desert. Nobody has to walk it alone. That's the week.
